Mr. GEORGE PARENT, Quebec West, (for Mr. Jacobs) presented the second report of the select standing committee on public accounts as follows:
The select standing committee on public accounts beg leave to present the following as their second report:
Your committee now have under consideration certain items contained in the Auditor
General's report for the fiscal year _ ending March 31st, 1928, as referred to the =aid committee.
It is deemed advisable by your committee that certain other items which are contained in the Auditor General's report for the previous year also be taken under consideration. Your committee therefore recommend that the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ending March 31st, 1927, be referred to the said committee.
Mr. Speaker, there is an apparent misunderstanding in connection with this report.

The hon. member should
give notice.

I am not opposing the motion, Your Honour. The hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent) is making this motion in place of the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). When the committee was in session yesterday I made two motions, and I think the hon. member for Quebec West has not quite grasped the import of what took place.
The first motion was for the production of material in connection with the Matane dredging contract. This matter dealt with items from the Auditor General's reports of 1924, 1925 and 1926, and it was then suggested that without leave of the house it would not be possible to have the reports for those three years taken up.
The second motion was in relation to the Beauchemin library, and dealt with extracts from the Auditor General's reports for the years 1926, 1927 and 1928.
In view of the fact that information is sought in regard to these matters, and the files relating to entries appearing in the Auditor General's report for those respective years are asked for, it was thought, that the house should be requested to refer to that committee all of the entries and all the files relating to the various years. The hon. member for Cartier undertook to bring that matter up and place it before the house. I am quite satisfied that that was his intention but he has been unexpectedly called away, and I am asking now that the hon. member for Quebec West place the matter before the house.

Under the circumstances,
I think the motion had better stand.

May I draw this
to your attention, Mr. Speaker:	My information from the hon. member for Cartier is that owing to certain religious observances in which he is at present concerned, it will not be possible for him to be present in the house until some time next week. I think the work of the committee should not suffer
Public Accounts Committee

meanwhile, and I am quite sure the hon. member for Quebec West will concur with me that the matter is as I have stated. Therefore I ask that the motion may be so altered as to enable the committee to go on with its very necessary work.

The motion had better
stand.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Since the motion has been
called, a rather serious situation has developed. I am not saying at the moment that a deliberate endeavour has been made to prevent investigation, but the fact is that two very prominent members on the opposite side of the house are energetically taking action that, if carried to its finality, would result in the investigations never being completed. I need hardly point out to the house that it has been a rule from time immemorial that when an item is under consideration in the public [DOT] accounts committee, you may trace it back to its origin without any further reference to the house. Unfortunately, however, the contention has been made-and a majority vote in the committee succeeded in carrying the views of that majority, of course-that you cannot investigate an item, the details of which appear in a previous auditor general's report, beyond the year preceding the year just ended. I need hardly say that such a contention, if carried to its finality, would render nugatory any effort made by the public accounts committee.
The rule, as I understand it-and I have asked some of the oldest members of the house-is perfectly clear, that if in the public accounts for the year ended March 31, 1928, there appears an item indicating that payments have been made to A. B. and it becomes necessary to trace the matter back to its origin, even as the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said, to confederation itself; if it is a continuous series of transactions, then you can trace it back to its origin without referring the matter to the house. That looks on the face of it so sensible as not to require discussion. The hon. gentleman who has made the motion has an entirely different view. He believes the house adopted another rule. I do not find any evidence of the adoption of such a rule. The public accounts are on the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) referred to the public accounts committee. It will be recalled that last year a little conversation took place with respect to that owing to the late date in the session at which the public accounts were referred; and without prejudice to our position. At the

moment, the motion of the hon. member for Quebec West is a motion intended to empower the committee to go back beyond the Auditor General's report for 1928 with respect to a certain related item, and of course the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will realize just what that means. You cannot carry on your discussion with respect to the final payment of an account unless you can go back to its origin and trace it down, because it is based on a contract either express or implied, a contract in writing or a verbal contract given by one of the departments. That may be five or six years ago. I know of one ten or eleven years back.
The Welland canal.

Yes, the Welland canal
contract was signed in-
There are a large number of Welland canal contracts dating back quite a number of years.

I thank the Minister of Railways. They go back at least six or seven years and they are being projected into the future. Suppose in 1929 the public accounts committee is investigating the accounts of March 31, 1928, with respect to any one of those contracts: I think the house has ruled time after time-and the committee has always thought it was so plain it was not necessary to come back to the house-that you can investigate from the origin of the contract down to the date you are then considering, on the assumption, of course, that the matter has not been previously investigated, and if so, the details are available. Payments of public moneys are authorized either under statute or by contract. There may be a written contract or sometimes only a verbal contract and the duty of the public accounts committee is to investigate the soundness of the payments; whether they were warranted or not; whether the prices paid were reasonable; whether tenders were called; whether the moneys voted and paid reached the source indicated by the account or some other source. The public accounts committee is endeavouring to function, not as a party machine, but for the purpose of indicating to the people of Canada whether or not the money is properly expended in accordance with the will of parliament. If it has not been, this committee is going to ascertain that fact. The mere fact that the chairman of the committee is absent to-day or to-morrow should not be a reason for holding up the matter. Summer will come and winter too, if we are going to have only one meeting of the committee a week and then

Public Accounts Committee
have it met by such a motion as that which has been considered during the last few days. For that reason, I think the observations made by the hon. member for West Hamilton, which indicate that a certain resolution was to be submitted to the house because a majority of the committee determined that it would be against all precedent-
No.
There was no vote in the committee at all.
I was in the committee and I opposed it throughout.
There was no vote.
No, but I opposed it throughout.
The ayes and nays were called.
On every occasion where it has been possible the majority of the committee has been summoned to prevent these investigations from being carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I ask the minister to read the record. I know what he has seen in his experience in connection with public accounts. The committee has now adjourned until next Wednesday. On Wednesday an effort will be made to have it meet on Thursday alt ten o'clock, and on Friday at ten o'clock. Surely hon. members remember that the public accounts committee, when an opposition was investigating the Arctic accounts, sat for days and weeks and it dragged into a month before they got all the horrid details brought to the attention of the public. We are going to endeavour to do the same thing this year and to do so means that the will of a majority is not going to impose itself against the right to investigate the public accounts of Canada which represent moneys paid by the people of Canada and not by any one party. Let that be clearly understood.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Alinister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I fail to see just exactly what the leader of the opposition has been asking for. I understood that the request of the hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) was that a certain report, which is before the house at the moment, should be amended before it is accepted.
To carry out an agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is a matter of changing the wording of a report, and
a report that was signed by the chairman. The chairman happens to be absent at the moment; but if my hon. friend will permit me the time necessary to telephone him,
I will endeavour to get his consent to make a change that is a matter, as I gather it, not of any consequence beyond that of having the committee meet, if possible, at an earlier date.

May I interrupt the Prime Minister just a moment? As the Prime Minister rose to his feet, I think the hon. member for Quebec West was about to say something further, and possibly he was about to express his acquiescence in what I had asked for. If that is the case, we can make progress.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If other members of the committee are agreeable, it will facilitate matters, but the chairman who signed the document ought to know, before that document is changed, if there is an intention to alter it. I should not think we would be losing very much time if the motion were to stand over for another day. If it can be settled at the moment, so much the better. I object, however, to my hon. friend taking advantage of a discussion of the kind when a certain courtesy is being asked of the government-

It is not a courtesy; it
is a matter of right.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Do not insult the members of the committee.
Air. A1ACKENZIE KING:	I do not see
why my hon. friend the leader of the opposition should lose his temper over it. It is not as serious as all that. The government is entirely in accord with the view of my hon. friend that the public accounts should be investigated whenever it is thought desirable to have them investigated, and that the fullest opportunity for investigation should be given. No one takes any other view.
They act the other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a most unfair reflection.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is possible that we can arrange to meet my hon. friend in the way that has been suggested, but if the other members of the committee have some substantial reason for not acquiescing in my hon. friend's request at the moment, we shall have to ask him to let the matter stand until to-morrow, and in the interval I will get into communication with the chairman of the committee.
Public Accounts Committee
Mr. Speaker, may I say-

The horn gentleman has
already spoken.
I am only speaking in answer to what the Prime Minister has just said. Is that out of order, Mr. Speaker?
Yes.

I think by unanimous
consent we might hear the hon. gentleman.

I
would like to say a word in answer to the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). Having been a member of the public accounts committee for many years, I strongly resent the hon. leader of the opposition insinuating or seeking to create the impression in this house that the public accounts committee are trying to prevent hon. members on the other side of the house from investigating in the committee any matter in connection with the public accounts. There is no such intention and there has been no such action on the part of any members of that committee since I have been a member of it, and that is a good many years now.
The report which has been presented by the chairman was discussed last Wednesday before the public accounts committee, and my recollection is that the committee unanimously consented to this reference to the house because some members of the committee thought that we did not have power to go into the public accounts of years gone by. The chairman himself stated that he did not think we had that power. The committee therefore agreed that we should refer back to this house and seek authority to investigate the public accounts of years gone by and go into the files. I wish to repeat that there has been no intention on the part of the committee, and no action taken, to try and prevent a thorough investigation of any item in the public accounts.

As a member of the public accounts committee, I was present throughout the whole discussion yesterday, when not only did various members on the other side of the house sitting on that committee take the attitude that we could not examine further back than the present Auditor General's report, but the Solicitor General himself (Mr. Cannon), a member of the government, stated that the reference of the house to the committee concerned only the Auditor General's report which is lying on

the table at the present time; that is, for the year 1927-1928. That was the attitude of the whole party on the other side of the house sitting on that committee-absolutely.	I
argued against that at considerable length, as did others, and in the end, because the government members were in the majority and we could not do anything else, we agreed to refer back to the house for a ruling.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	Before my hon.
friend sits down, I would like to ask him if there was any objection on the part of any members of the committee to securing what they regarded as the necessary authority, namely, a reference by the house of the accounts in question?

There was objection
throughout to going further back than the present Auditor General's report without first coming back to this house for a reference.

As a member of that committee, I desire to support what the last speaker (Mr. Manion) has said, and to say a word in answer to the remark made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe)-"most unfair, most unfair." I would like to point out to the house the treatment that was accorded by that committee. It is true that by a majority vote at the meeting just previous to the last one we asked that we should be allowed to examine the files in relation to a contractor named MacMillan, whom I do not know, in regard to a matter in connection with Bedford basin. We said that we desired the file in order to find out the nature of the case, and to examine the officers of the department so as to have a complete story of the matter. The position taken by the majority on the other side, of course, was that we could not do this, that we could not find out whether there was a proper case or not to allege against MacMillan unless we had MacMillan himself present.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, should the hon. member discuss the proceedings of the committee when the particular matter on which he is speaking is not before the house? The question before us is a motion to extend the jurisdiction of the committee.

I understand that the
hon. gentleman is simply giving an illustration in leading up to his point that at the last meeting of the committee the opportunity was not given to the minority, I suppose, which they desired. The hon. gentleman will please come to the point.

Public Accounts Committee

I will come to the point, Mr. Speaker, which is this, that a majority of that committee by a vote of nineteen to fourteen said that we were not to be allowed to examine the files or call the officers of the department and ascertain whether or not there was a case until we had Mr. MacMillan present.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to correct an
impression which the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) left on this house.
I understood him to say that the committee by a majority vote had taken a certain decision last Wednesday. I am a member of the committee and was present at the meeting of the committee. The hon. leader of the opposition was not present. The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) made a motion for the production of certain papers and certain files relating to a certain account, and the question was raised-it was put by myself to the chairman of the committee, for information-as to the rule that should govern in such cases. In the course of the discussion two points were raised: First, whether it was within the power of the public accounts committee to discuss items beyond two years back; second, whether the committee could go beyond the order of reference from this house. Earlier in the session the public accounts as contained in the Auditor General's report for the year ending March 31, 1928, were referred to the public accounts committee, and the question raised in the committee was whether the committee could go beyond that order of reference. Those were the two points raised.
There was no vote taken in the committee one way or the other. The chairman was of the opinion that the committee could not go beyond its order of reference and it was the general agreement of the committee that if it did not have sufficient power to go into the accounts that were desired to be examined, it should come back to this house for an extension of its power. There was no suggestion of blocking inquiry in any way, shape or form. There was no vote taken one way or the other with regard to the matter.

As a member of the public accounts committee, I resent very much what the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has said with regard to supposed obstruction by some members of that committee. I am for fairness in discussion, and for nothing being hidden in connection with the committee's inquiry. I move that not only should MacMillan appear before the committee, but also the
Minister of National Defence in the Meighen government of 1926, the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), and the Minister of Railways and Canals in the same government, the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black); that they should be invited to appear before the committee to explain why they stopped the contract, afterwards gave orders to the contractor to resume the work, and later cancelled the contract. I think they should explain their action to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, if I understand aright the difficulty which has arisen, it appears to me that a majority of the committee was of opinion that the committee could not inquire into anything beyond the single Auditor General's report which was referred to the committee on the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). It has always been a rule that any item in that particular report may be inquired into and may be traced to its inception, no matter how far back it goes. But I agree that a new investigation should not be started in regard to an item which appears in past reports of the Auditor General, but which does not appear at all in the particular report under consideration by the committee. But that, Mr. Speaker, is fundamental. Surely the committee does not require instructions in regard to it. With all due respect, I think the majority of the committee has acted very strangely in bringing the matter before the house at all. If an item is in the report which has been referred to the committee, that item can be traced back to its inception, and it has been the custom for the last thirty years to do so. But I do not think the committee has the right, unless specially directed, to inquire into items which do not appear in the last report referred to it; that is, the committee cannot rake up matters contained in former reports of the Auditor General unless those matters are specially referred to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not a member of the public accounts committee and I do not know what happened there. I have nothing to say about its proceedings but my friend from East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) has taken exception to the words I uttered, "most unfair". I was not referring to anything that has happened in the committee, but to the words of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition when he said that Liberal members were summoned to attend the public accounts committee for the purpose of preventing the proposals of my hon. friendis opposite being adopted. I thought

Public Accounts Committee
those words most unfair, and I still think so. The members of the public accounts committee who happen to be sitting on this side of the house have a duty to discharge in that committee, as well as my hon. friends opposite. It is their duty to attend there, and it is unfair to reflect on their attendance. It is rather difficult to please my hon. friend, for I remember last year when a certain committee was sitting he complained twice or three times in the house that Liberal members of that committee deliberately refrained from attending its sittings. This year he is complaining because they are attending. I think-
That was to make a quorum.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think those words
are unfair, and I still protest against them.
I desire to correct a statement made by the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe).
Order.
Order.

This is a question of
privilege. The Minister of Justice said that last session I complained because Liberal members did not attend the committee. I complained of their non-attendance at that time because there was not a quorum, and there could not be one unless they attended. Why did they stay away?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is a great difference.

I desire, Mr. Speaker,
to concur in the view expressed by the hon. member for South Wellington-with all due deference to the chairman of the committee,
I suppose we can all have views on the matter under discussion-to the extent that wherever an item appears in the current public accounts, and its source is in the public accounts of previous years it is competent for the committee to follow that item back to its source. But may I point out that so far from this report being a reflection on the motives of the majority of the committee, the report itself, if adopted, will go much further than my hon. friends opposite desire to go,-
No.

-because apparently not only will it permit the committee to trace the items which appear in the current public accounts back to their source, but it will also permit the committee to go into any other items which appear in the previous public accounts mentioned in the report. That is my reason for objecting to the unfairness of

the insinuation

shall I say?-which emanated from the ether side in regard to the matter. Without at all debating whether or not the items in the present public accounts can be traced back to their source, at least the majority of the committee desired the house to place every facility at the disposal of the committee.
You were not at the committee.

I hold in my hand the
report of the proceedings, and I will read it into Hansard for the information of the house. When motives are called in question the actual language used surely can be quoted. Let me read from the report:
It is deemed advisable by your committee that certain other items which are contained in the Auditor General's report for the previous year also be taken under consideration. Your committee therefore recommend that the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1927, be referred to the said committee.
This is, the whole report for the previous year.

Mr. Speaker-, while agreeing with the views of both the member for South Wellington and the Minister of Railways with respect to the logical procedure in matters of this kind, I must disagree with the implication of the last remarks of the Minister of Railways. I am wondering to myself what is going to happen if, every time an examination of an item that comes before the public accounts committee discloses that its source is to be found in previous accounts, that committee is to have to come before this house-
No.

Just a
moment; if that committee has to come before this house for an extension of power.

My hon. friend will
surely permit me to say that in my opinion- and I am not the judge; I presume the Speaker is-such a return to this house is not necessary, provided the item in question has its origin in previous public accounts.
That is what we have said.
With that I agree; but the implication in the latter part of my hon. friend's remarks would lead us to believe that the majority of the committee had met that situation and gone much further.
It has.

I may be
entirely wrong, but I hold the view that if

Public Accounts Committee
the house adopts this ^report it will create a precedent which will require on every subsequent examination of accounts, other than those of the current year, that the committee must come back to this house in order to gets its powers extended for the purpose of such examination. If it is to be regarded as a precedent, I must object to it, not because I am a member of the committee but because I do not think it is the proper procedure. I do not think it is logical, nor do I think it will facilitate the work of the committee. If it is not to be regarded as a precedent, well and good.

Mr. Speaker, as a private member of the house-I am not a member of the public accounts committee-as soon as the report was read I at once intended bringing to your attention what I conceive to be a very serious principle involved in the report. As I understand the situation, it is this. It has been ruled by the chairman of the public accounts committee that it is not competent for the committee to examine into files on matters beyond the single year contained jin the Auditor General's report, in this case covering the fiscal year ending March 31, 1928. I submit to Your Honour that the members of the public accounts committee have a perfect right to request production of the files and to examine officers of whatever department may be involved in regard to any item included in that year's report, and to follow that item as many years as it goes back in the records of parliament. If that is the case, then the submission to parliament to-day is unnecessary. If the adoption of this report is to be accepted as establishing the ruling of the chairman of the committee that it was not competent for the committee to go back beyond the current report of the Auditor General without a further reference to the house, then I would oppose very, very strongly the adoption of the report. And that is the understanding which we on this side of the house have of the ruling of the chairman of the committee. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has made what I conceive to be a perfectly proper interpretation of the rule, namely, that it is competent for the committee to follow an item back without reference whatsoever to the house; and if the house agrees to that then, so far as I am concerned, I have nothing more to say on the subject. If, on the other hand, the adoption of the report nullifies the opinion expressed by the minister, who is not at the moment leading, then it is a very serious matter.
I think I intimated that it was the Speaker who would determine the rule.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):
speechtext:
The objection to the report, it seems to me, is this:	It must be admitted
that when any item in the present Auditor General's Report is under consideration, which relates to an antecedent contract running through two or three prior years, the committee has the undoubted power and authority to proceed to investigate the antecedents of that item, if it is, for example, a continuing contract or a contract on which payments were made, say, three years ago, the final payment falling within the last Auditor General's Report. You have the right to trace the item back to the initiation of the contract under which it arose. That seems to be conceded by the Minister of Railways. Now this resolution assumes, first, that the committee cannot investigate any item further back than the year which has just closed.
I read it carefully-
I have it before me.
-and I find in it no reference-

I find in it a clear intimation or implication to that effect. The report states:
It is deemed advisable by your committee that certain other items which are contained in the Auditor General's report for the previous year also be taken under consideration.
That, if it passed, would create, it seems to me, the clear implication that although the item which appears in this last annual report might be investigated, it could be investigated only in case that the previous Auditor General's report is brought before the 'committee. And it is that implication which we oppose in this report. If it is the clear understanding that when an item has arisen in the last Auditor General's report, relating to a continuing contract, that item should be or may be investigated by the committee back to the last year and to the preceding year, or for any number of years until you reach the source from which the item arose-until you reach the contract under which it arose- then the case is different. It is therefore the implication in this report, that the committee cannot go beyond the last year unless by order of the house, to which we take exception. It is suggested that under the proposed order you could not go back beyond the second preceding year, whereas, as a matter of practice in this house, the item should if necessary be traced to its origin.
Public Accounts Committee

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think it has been made quite clear from this side of the house that we do not differ at all from hon. gentlemen opposite in the view that any item being investigated by the public accounts committee may be traced back to any number of years. That is perfectly clear. With respect to this particular report, we on this side of the house, might take the view if we wished to be unduly suspicious, that hon. gentlemen opposite in not wishing to have the report adopted, see some desire on the part of Liberals to have some items which appear in the 1927 report and which do not appear in the 1928 report not referred to the committee for investigation, because of what the investigation may lead to. I do . not think that any purpose of that kind is contemplated. The committee was genuine in wanting to clear up to the satisfaction of everyone the difference of view which took place the other day, and if we are agreed on the main point, that an item may be traced back to its source, and that this report was brought down with a view of helping to make that possible in order to remove any difficulties in that direction, we may adopt the report.
No, withdraw the report; otherwise, as my right hon. friend will see, it limits investigation to 1927 and 1928.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. It may be that the majority would like to have that particular report referred to the committee-
It is now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, that is
the 1927 report. The 1928 report is the one which has been referred to the committee. I hope my hon. friend does not want to be placed in the position of preventing the 1927 report from being referred to the committee.

Did not the Prime
Minister, at the last session, say that there would be no objection to considering items in the Auditor General's report, 1926 and 1927? That is covered by the motion, and so long as it is understood, and the Prime Minister's statement implements that understanding, there is no quarrel.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I not only said it last session but I say it now, and would be prepared to say it again next year.

Is it not a fact that certain members of the committee have asked for the production of documents which are referred to, not in the 1928 Auditor General's report but in the 1927 report, items which have not their origin in 1928? If that is the case, the resolution I submit is a perfectly proper one.
I am not in a position to answer the hon. gentleman's question, but the chairman of the committee no doubt knows. The hon. gentleman himself was present and he would know.
I was not there yesterday.

But it is perfectly clear now-and we are agreed on this point-that the only question is as regards the language of the motion. It is desirable to have the motion so worded that it shall not be a precedent which would make it appear necessary to come back to this house to get authority to investigate items to their source.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have asked from the beginning that the motion stand.
In view of the fact that the chairman is absent, and as the Prime Minister has properly said he has signed something which he might not desire to have someone else amend, the motion might stand.

The report cannot be
amended by the house but there may be a motion to refer it back to the committee with a view to its amendment in certain respects.
I understand that it is the wish of the house that the motion stand, but if it is intended that the report be amended it must be referred back to the committee. Bourinot says:
A report may he referred back to a committee for further consideration, or with instructions giving them power to amend the same in any respect.

Someone who was present
yesterday must know what happened.

Not always.

Questions
Surely some member of the committee can tell us whether or not the items which are required to be discussed had their origin in the 1928 report.
It has not been suggested here that it was so.

I understood the wish of
the house was that the motion should stand.

I move the adjournment of
the debate.

It is moved by Mr
Ernst, seconded by Mr. Barber, that the debate on the motion be adjourned. If the debate is not adjourned, hon. members who have already spoken might speak again to-morrow.
Motion stands.

On section 2-Application of Railway Act and Expropriation Act to company.

I mentioned this matter
the other day. It is very difficult for the small property owners bo have recourse to the exchequer court, and these matters could be more readily dealt with by the county or dis-
C.N.R. Act Amendment

trict judge. I gather from the amendment which the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has said he proposes to move that he thinks the suggestion is meritorious. I mentioned $1,000 the other day, but the minister proposes to make that sum $2,500, so that the exchequer court will deal with all cases in which the amount exceeds $2,500. I think that is a very good solution, because the $2,500 will bring these cases within the jurisdiction of the supreme court and if a litigant felt that there was some great principle at stake he could take an appeal to that court.
The amendment contains the words, "where the claim does not exceed $2,500." That is rather indefinite because a man might claim $5,000 and the government might make an offer of $2,000. I think it should be made absolutely clear and the test should be certain. As it now stands I do not think the test is certain, because we do not know to whose claim this refers.
In order to get the matter before the committee, Mr. Chairman, I move the amendment which the leader of the opposition has just referred to.

Will the minister read it,
please?

It would be an addition following the word "thereof" in the eleventh line of subsection (d) of section 2, and reads as follows:
Provided that such compensation may in any ease where a claim does not exceed $2,500, be ascertained under the provisions of the Railway act beginning with notice of expropriation to the opposite party.
I discussed the point just raised by the leader of the opposition with the law officers from the point of view of the actual operation of such a procedure, and I am advised that "beginning with notice of expropriation to the opposite party" does immediately involve the making of a claim for compensation by the opposite party. We are therefore making the amount $2,500 based upon the claim made by the party who is being expropriated. I raised the amount to $2,500, having in mind the factor to which my hon. friend referred, namely, that it would allow greater latitude while at the same time leaving the operation of the amendment to be based upon the claim of the party whose property was being expropriated, rather than upon the action of the company who was expropriating.
[Mr. Bennett.J

Would it not be better
to say " Where the claim of the owner does not exceed $2,500," and thereby remove any possible doubt as to the meaning of the language?

I defer to my hon.
friend's legal knowledge in that regard, but, as he is aware, in expropriation proceedings other factors than ownership enter.
I know.

I am therefore afraid of complicating the language. The use of the term " opposite party " later on is intended to apply generally and to include owners or tenants or any others who might have an interest in the property. Probably my hon. friend would examine the amendment.

I have examined it. The point that I desire to make is that the term " opposite party " does not convey the meaning the minister desires to have us understand. I should think we want to make it perfectly clear that where a claimant sets up a demand for more than $2,500, he must go to the exchequer court, but where the demand does not exceed $2,500, the matter may be heard by the district court under the provisions of the Railway Act. The amendment reads:
Beginning with the notice of expropriation by the opposite party.
Should that not be " by the railway company?"

The wording is:
Beginning with notice of expropriation to the opposite party.
That has reference also to the provisions of the Railway Act.

I think it would be
better if it read:	"Notice of expropriation
by the railway company." As my hon. friend will recall, this is the practice: first of all, the plan is filed at the registry office. Then notice is given of intention to take, indicating how much money will be paid. The owners ' or those interested, if dissatisfied, may go to the district court to have that compensation assessed. The difficulty is that the claim must not exceed $2,500, but the man has no opportunity to set up his claim until after the government or, at least, the railway, has filed its plan. The notice to take is the first step; then there is the opportunity to decide upon the sufficiency of the offer. The claimant has the option of indicating that he will not accept the amount offered, and that he requires a larger sum. Would it not be better

C.N.R. Act Amendment
to say: "After notice has been given by the railway company of expropriation," rather than " to the opposite party?" In that case you have no doubt that it begins from the time you give notice.

I am looking up the
sections of the Railway Act. I always hesitate to change a purely legal draft without being sure of my ground. Section 215 of the Railway Act is the section dealing with the matter. It reads:
Preliminary to proceeding to arbitration to fix compensation or damages the company shall serve upon the opposite party-
The same language is used, you see.
-a notice, which shall contain
(a)	a description of the lands to be taken, or of the powers intended to be exercised with regard to any lands therein described;
(b)	a declaration of readiness to pay a certain sum or rent, as the case may be, as compensation for such lands or for such damages; and
(e) a notification that if -within ten days after the service of this notice, or, where the notice is served by publication, within one month after the first publication thereof, the party to whom the notice is addressed does not give notice to the company that he accepts the sum offered by the company, either he or the company will be entitled to apply to have the compensation fixed by arbitration as provided in this act.
Apparently what the officers had in mind was to transfer the option of placing the case before the exchequer court or the district court to the claimant, rather than to retain that option themselves. I think that has merit.
I am not objecting to that, but does the provision make it clear that a claim which a man sets up for $5,000 ha? to go to the exchequer court, although he might ultimately receive $2,000?
I think that is clear.
Is that what it is intended to do?
Yes.

Having regard to the fact that this country is so large and the facilities of treating with matters in the exchequer court are so limited, when you fix $2,500 as the criterion, as the minister has done, I think it is an exceedingly fair proposition. That will meet most of the cases I had in mind the other day. But I think it should be fixed in the statute itself as being either the sum offered by the railway company on the one hand, or claimed by the owner on the other. As the matter stands now, the man who might
claim $3,000 would have to go to the exchequer court although he might be awarded $2,500. I am only suggesting to the minister, in the light- of my experience, that it is hardly fair to ask persons from whom land has to be taken by expropriation, that they should go to the exchequer court. It is too expensive; it requires the employment of solicitors and lawyers to deal with forms and procedure, whereas the other method is very simple. I have known many men conduct their cases successfully before district courts and while I do not desire in any sense to delay the minister's legislation, it seems to me it would be preferable to say " where the sum offered by the railway company does not exceed $2,500." In other words, the law officers of the minister's department have told him to put the onus on the unfortunate owner. I suggest that it is rather desirable to put it- on the railway company. I only do that because, as the minister himself realizes, in a province as large as Saskatchewan, for instance, there are many cases in which a man has his land taken from him by the railway, values it at three or four thousand dollars, and may get only $2,500, and the costs in exchequer court proceedings would be very considerable, and the court only goes to that country once a year. I do not think it conduces to the orderly conduct of affairs, in view of the small sums of money affected in this way, to put the onus on the individual I leave it entirely to the minister, but if the responsibility were mine, I think I would prefer to put it the other way and let the sum tendered by the railway company be the determining factor.

I confess to the committee that the sum suggested to me by the law officers of the railway was less than $2,500. It was in fact $600, to correspond with the normal jurisdiction of the district court judge
They have a jurisdiction of $1,000 in some of the provinces.

I do not know much
law, but I happen to know-and this I pointed out to them-that strangely enough the district court judge apparently had wider financial jurisdiction under the Railway Act than under the act setting up his court in the first place. That is an anomaly that presently exists. Therefore I saw no reason to adopt any standard contained in any district court act, but for the reason advanced by my hon. friend I would rather raise the limit in favour of the claimant. With regard to $2,500, what I have in mind is the usual small expropriation for right of way which involves the
C.N.R. Act Amendment

crossing of a farm. There are very few farm crossings nowadays that take any such sum as $2,500. I had in mind that general situation in setting the sum.
Apparently the only point my hon. friend asks me to consider is whether I should not go a little bit further and make the basis that the jurisdiction should be determined rather by the offer made by the railway company than by the claim made by the owner. I would like to hear that point discussed a little further, if other hon. gentlemen who have had experience with these expropriation matters would give me their advice. I am quite open-minded about it, with this one qualification: More and more the exchequer court of Canada, in connection with small cases, is using that provision of the Exchequer Court Act or Expropriation Act which permits them to have hearings held by delegates of the court, rather than by the court itself sitting in different parts of the country. That practice is growing, and wisely I think, in connection with small expropriation claims. That is to say, the exchequer court may delegate a district court judge to hear the case, the district court judge not deciding it, but referring his evidence and his opinion thereon to the exchequer court, which in turn renders the decision.

I doubt very much if
they have any power to do that in this
case.
Not under the Exchequer Court Act?

I know, but this is the
appointment of a tribunal to deal with a definite matter. That tribunal is the exchequer court, and the judgment must be a judgment of that court. That is one of the reasons why I pointed out to the minister the desirability of making it as easy as possible, because the poor unfortunate who fails in his claim will have nothing left, because of there being so much machinery to put in action. Although the exchequer court holds local sittings at various towns and cities in Canada, it is domiciled, so to speak, in Ottawa. It was that which prompted my suggestion the other day. I think the minister has met it exceedingly fairly. But I still doubt, having regard to the very great area of Canada and to the fact that there is but one court with two judges, whether it is desirable to fix the jurisdiction at $2,500 as the sum offered by the railway company, and if any greater sum is offered by the railway company, recourse can be had to the exchequer court.

If it is less than $2,500, the claimant can avail himself of the provision of the Railway Act. I do not think that is unfair. But the minister is charged with responsibility in connection with this matter. The money comes out of the people of the country in the long run.

I am prepared to adopt
for a moment the comfortable position of a judge on the bench and listen to argument. I am willing to make either decision in the judgment of this committee. If my hon friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary) has any suggestion to make, I shall be pleased to hear it. Personally I think there is a difference of opinion between the lawyers themselves,

May I say, without trespassing too much on the time of the committee, thgt usually in arriving at the sum to be offered, the railway company is governed by the report of the engineers and appraisers. They realize that the responsibility is theirs, having compulsorily taken the land in the first instance, and they usually desire to ensure that they will not be compelled to pay a larger sum than they offer. I have been engaged in many of these cases both for the railway companies and the owners. I recall the entrance of the Grand Trunk into Calgary, in connection with which I acted for a very largei number of small owners, some of whose lots it split in two. The railway company offered what they conceived to be a fair land value, but it was not adequate compensation for the lots, and the owners succeeded in getting a somewhat larger sum. I am speaking merely in the public interest in this matter, and I am sure the minister wants to place on the statute books a provision that will work no hardship to any honest claimant, at the same time protecting the public treasury from settlements that are forced, so to speak, by reason of local or other pressure that may be brought to bear in connection with matters of this kind. The local tribunal is a very complete answer, as the minister knows, because the county court judge understands the situation better than a person not residing in the locality.

It seems to me that you are on sounder ground in basing the jurisdiction on the value made by the company rather than by the claimant. I think experience shows that it is quite likely that in most cases the railway company will be more nearly right than the claimant's idea of what he should get. The company is also better versed in the procedure, and better versed in judging what is going to result from the

Supply-Public Works-Maritimes
evidence that is given, and as to the sort of award the court is likely to make. So it seems to me that the company's estimate of damage is more likely to be right than is the estimate of the claimant, and I think you are on a sounder basis if you take the company's proposition up to $2,500 as being the basis of jurisdiction, rather than taking the claim made by a man who may have very exaggerated ideas as to the value of his land, and who who may be kept out of this simple court because his ideas are exaggerated.

And the responsibility
for going into the other court will always be his, if you have it the way we suggest.

The officers of the company who deal with these matters advise me that the most extraordinarily exaggerated demands for compensation arise mainly in connection with small compensation claims- that the larger the actual amount involved, the less the degree of exaggeration in the claim of the claimant. That is the broad experience.
That is natural too.

Yes, and I have no doubt that the officers, in considering it, had in mind that the legal advisers of the claimant would pay due regard to the court before which the claimant would have to appear in the first instance and present his claim in connection with these small amounts. However, in order not to take up further time, as my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is anxious and ready to go on. I would suggest that we follow this course: strike out the word "claim" in the second line of the amendment, and insert instead the words "offer of the company." With this understanding, that we will report the bill out of committee and leave it for third reading in order that I may make absolutely sure that no complication will arise as a result of the amendment.

I think that will oover
it.

I do not question the
legal advice of my hon. friend, but he will understand my desire to get the legal advice of the officers of the department.

I think that entirely
covers the situation, Mr. Chairman. I quite appreciate the minister's position. His duty is to take responsibility on the advice of his legal officers, and we do not happen at the moment to be in that happy position. If on third reading it is thought desirable we can again deal with the amendment.

The Prime Minister will realize what I have in mind when I point this out. We are now endeavouring to establish a research department and I have been looking into the matter to ascertain what duplication there is. The minister will observe that we are providing for a laboratory of hygiene and a laboratory in connection with mines and minerals, and the new building discussed last year was to deal with certain other matters in connection with forest products which are being tested. Now the question is whether or not there is duplication of activities in the various departments. Why. for instance, should the Minister of Public Works deal with the matter of machines in the post office? Take that $26,000 for equipment in connection with the post office. Is this for the new machines that have been patented, for the purpose of lessening the amount of manual labour which has to be done, and which machines are merely leased and not bought? I ask this question because this is the only means whereby we may get information on the subject.

There is no departure
from the practice that has been followed with regard to the fitting of post office buildings. This item of $60,000 is required for the purchase and installation of metal file cases, shelving and other fittings needed in the parliamentary and departmental offices in Ottawa.

Ottawa. It is considered that this equipment will cost approximately $26,000. 1 am bringing this matter to your attention in case you may be able to place an item in the supplementary estimates to provide for the work.

There has been no request, so far as I know, for a renewal of the equipment the hon. member speaks of.

I have already referred
to installations in connection with various laboratories. I shall have something to say in regard to dredging and the advisability of
having some central organization in connection with the conduct of public affairs, but I will not go into that matter at the moment. Just now I am dealing with laboratories and other buildings of that character. We cannot possibly get along if each department claims the right to have one of these establishments; we cannot possibly make progress under such conditions in a country such as this. We are establishing this new department of research, about which we are all so anxious and which will serve useful purposes in this country, and what I want to point out in this connection is this: We are voting public money to establish, in several other branches of the service, undertakings which ultimately must be regarded as research in the true sense of the term, and I for one am opposed to that being done. I mentioned the matter last year when the Prime Minister was discussing the matter of research activities. We are engaged, for instance, in wood testing and activities of that sort, all desirable, all admirable in their way. But the Prime Minister having invited suggestions as to how public money might be saved, I suggest that we prevent duplication wherever possible; in other words, that a well organized department should take care of the very work which at present is being done in several departments of the public service. I do not think it is conducive to the public interest that one particular service should set up a research department of its own for testing purposes, say, another department do the same, and still another. We are endeavouring now to consolidate our activities, and while one could understand such duplication at one time :t should now be avoided. I am not saying this in any critical or censorious spirit; I say it because I have been investigating the matter and I find that there is on the part of officials a tendency, which after all is but human, not to let go what they now have. I do not think however that we should expend public money to erect buildings which will indicate, on the part of this parliament, a desire to have more than one department dealing with questions of research, however manifold may be the activities of the various departments. I cannot consider it desirable that the departments should engage in these various enterprises.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There is a
committee of the cabinet composed of ministers in whose departments research work is carried on, and the object of the committee is to centralize as much as possible all research work of the government. The committee has been considering this whole matter very fully having in mind the establishment at an early date of the new industrial and scientific research laboratories, and I can assure my hon. friend that these particular requests, especially from one or two of the departments, have been examined in relation to the larger equipment for which arrangements have been made. There is a special reason, which the Minister of the Interior would be able to give if he were here as to why one or two laboratories separately existing should continue so to exist, but I can assure my hon. friend that the government is entirely of his view with regard to consolidating scientific and industrial research work and will prevent, as far as possible, any overlapping of the service in that regard.

I am sure the country
will receive the statement just made by the Prime Minister with great satisfaction, but a laboratory of hygiene, for instance, is perhaps one of the matters with which a well organized research bureau would think it had a great deal to do as a branch of its activities. In putting up these buildings I fear we may be promoting what I might call the sense of an independent branch of the public service rather than a coordinated branch having to do with research work. That is the point which I endeavoured to make, although I have not made it very clear. Perhaps we will ask the Minister of the Interior about the workshops, the mines and the forest products.
It seems to me that the Department of the Interior is hardly the department under which one would expect forest products testing operations to be carried on, for instance, because so far as the local situation is concerned the companies interested usually look after that work. However, I believe that with respect to export business this work has been very valuable; I might mention the work which has been done in connection with the tensile strengths of woods and so on. I should think that work would be very properly under the Department of Trade and Commerce,. and that is the reason I ventured to bring this matter to the attention of the house at this time. The observations of the Prime Minister quite assure me that the government are desirous of doing what I think most thoughtful Canadians desire in 
this regard, but to vote money for these separate buildings will put them in a bad way when they begin the work of consolidation. Many difficulties will be interposed; I am sure that during his investigations my right hon. friend has ascertained how difficult it is to overcome that great jealousy possessed by men which will not let them surrender any of their activities in connection with scientific work. The jealousy with which men will hold on to their little positions in an endeavour to maintain an organization is amazing, and these four items struck me as being so related to the large activities to which this country has very properly committed itself that I venture this criticism in the hope that the minister would lend himself to the expenditure of public money in such a way as to afford a foundation for the effort which will be made later on not to coordinate but rather to maintain independent organizations.
